label: Pleomorphic_Adenoma
answer_markdown:
## Key Facts
- Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign salivary gland tumor.
- Typically affects the parotid gland but can occur in other salivary glands.
- Characterized by a mix of epithelial and stromal (myxoid, chondroid) components.
- Surgical excision with a clear margin is curative; local recurrence occurs if incompletely excised.
- Transformation to carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma is rare.

## Terminology
- Synonyms: Benign mixed tumor.

## Clinical Issues
- Occurs in the parotid gland in 65-80% of cases.
- Presents as a painless, slow-growing mass.
- Peak incidence in middle-aged adults; slight female predominance.

## Microscopic
- Triphasic pattern: Ductal epithelial cells, myoepithelial cells, and stromal component.
- Stroma: Typically myxoid, chondroid, or myxochondroid texture.
- Well-demarcated, encapsulated lesions.

## Ancillary Tests
- Immunohistochemistry often shows positivity for cytokeratins and S-100 in myoepithelial cells.
- PLAG1 gene rearrangements may be present.

## Differential Diagnosis
- **Basal Cell Adenoma** — Distinguished by basaloid biphasic pattern and lack of myxoid stroma.
- **Myoepithelioma** — Almost exclusive myoepithelial differentiation, lacking significant ductal structures.
- **Canalicular Adenoma** — Monomorphic histology, typically occurring in the upper lip.

For more detailed information, refer to [Pathology Outlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html).

cards.title: Salivary gland anlage tumour
cards.excerpt: Entity: Salivary gland anlage tumour definition: Salivary gland anlage tumour is a predominantly infantile nasopharyngeal lesion with biphasic squamoid epithelial and myoepithelial components continuous with the surface epithelium, resembling developing salivary gland. related_terminology: Not recommended: congenital pleomorphic adenoma. essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: a polypoid lesion with a complex network of ducts and solid-cystic squamous nests, showing continuity with surface squamous epithelium; hypocellular to cellular spindle cell stroma. Desirable: spindly cells positive for cytokeratins and SMA (in selected cases).

cards.title: Salivary gland myoepithelioma
cards.excerpt: Entity: Salivary gland myoepithelioma definition: Myoepithelioma (ME) is a benign salivary gland neoplasm that is composed almost exclusively of myoepithelial cells and the stroma they produce. related_terminology: Not recommended: myoepithelial cell tumour; myoepithelial adenoma. essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: almost exclusive myoepithelial differentiation and absence of invasion. Desirable: tumour encapsulation (except in minor salivary glands).

cards.title: Salivary gland myoepithelioma
cards.excerpt: Entity: Salivary gland myoepithelioma Section: differential_diagnosis The well-defined borders of the tumour and the lack of invasive growth distinguish ME from myoepithelial carcinoma. The characteristic basaloid biphasic pattern, peripheral palisading, and minimal to absent myxoid stroma of basal cell adenoma help to separate it from ME. Monomorphic histology and rare or absent ductal structures in ME separate it from pleomorphic adenoma. Distinguishing from soft tissue ME may be difficult, given the overlapping histological features and the presence of PLAG1 gene rearrangements in both.

cards.excerpt: Title: HN Lecture 1 Salivary1 Video ID: HN_Lecture_1_Salivary1 Primary tag: HN::Salivary::Cystadenoma_of_the_Salivary_Glands Tag status: semantic_gated_v0_2 Transcript: In cases of obstruction and a salivary retention cyst, amylase can crystallize. Crystallized amylase isn't particularly characteristic; people describe it as rhomboid, but the crystals are not uniformly rhomboid. Here is another large cyst with ciliated cell metaplasia. The other differential diagnosis for these ciliated cysts in the parotid (less commonly in the submandibular gland) is whether they are possibly a congenital remnant, specifically a branchial cleft cyst. However, the absence of lymphoid tissue typically associated with the epithelium in branchial cleft cysts argues against this. We are going to talk about lymphoepithelial sialadenitis, specifically the classic form.

cards.title: HN Lecture 2 Salivary2
cards.excerpt: Title: HN Lecture 2 Salivary2 Video ID: HN_Lecture_2_Salivary2 Primary tag: HN::Salivary_Gland::Malignant_Tumor::Adenoid_Cystic_Carcinoma Tag status: semantic_gated_v0_2 Transcript: Adenoid cystic carcinoma tends to be categorized among basaloid salivary gland tumors, often identified by its cytology. It features small cells, which should exhibit a distinct bilayer morphology unless there is high-grade transformation. Occasionally, myoepithelial cells may have clear cytoplasm, but this is not a universal feature. The tumor presents with cribriform, tubular, and solid growth patterns. A consistent finding in almost every case is basophilic, bubbly, blue-looking secretions within the lumina of the tubules or cribriform areas. Furthermore, perineural invasion is a hallmark of adenoid cystic carcinoma, and its absence should prompt questioning of the diagnosis. This is the bubbly stuff that looks kind of like blue cellophane, which is not ideal for discerning the blueness. I need to perform some color correction on that.

cards.excerpt: ..., it's important to differentiate primary salivary gland tumors from metastatic lesions. Metastatic cases may not undergo extensive surgery like a parotidectomy, due to the complexity of the facial nerve. For primary salivary gland neoplasms, while a specific diagnosis isn't always necessary, separating non-surgical from surgical neoplasms and grading them is vital. Low-grade neoplasms, including pleomorphic adenoma and low-grade malignancies, are usually managed with surgical resection.
